Should India standardise its air defence arsenal after Operation Sindoor?

Maj Gen (Dr) Ashok Kumar says he once believed in a "universal system." But experience changed his mind.

"One gun or one missile or one combination cannot address the multiple kinds of threats," he says.

From low-flying drones with tiny radar signatures to supersonic missiles and stand-off attacks by combat aircraft, "different kinds of threats require different kinds of matching" or, as he puts it, "horses for courses."

The real challenge, he argues, is finding the right balance: not too many systems, but enough capability to counter every threat while maximising indigenous production and sustainment.

This is a pivotal Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) meeting, not just because of its scale—₹52,000 crore in Capital Acceptances of Necessity (AoNs)—but because it marks a clear structural and doctrinal shift in Indian military procurement.

​Chaired by Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, this was the first DAC meeting following the recent major churn at the apex of India's military command structure, including the appointments of Chief of Defence Staff Gen Raja Subramani, Army Chief Gen Dhiraj Seth, and Navy Chief Adm Krishna Swaminathan.

​The influence of recent hostilities with Pakistan under Operation Sindoor is highly visible in these approvals. The lessons of that conflict—where low-cost drone swarms, loitering munitions, and electronic warfare clashed with conventional layered air defenses—have pushed India's acquisition priorities away from legacy, heavy conventional platforms and directly toward asymmetric, autonomous, and electronic warfare capabilities.

author: @AsYouNotWish
text:
Calling reports of India-Pakistan Track II engagement ‘PSYOP’ or propaganda is, to put it mildly, a bit rich.

The fact is that Track II dialogue between India and Pakistan never stopped. What stopped were official government-to-government talks. Those are not the same thing.

Track II has continued over the years through various forums involving former diplomats, military officers, intelligence veterans, academics and policy experts. During 2021 to January 2025, there were at least four such meetings in Muscat, Oman, alone, with participants from both sides. Only many of the individuals attending changed after Operation Sindoor. The process itself did not.

Which is why the denials now are difficult to take seriously. Track II was never the story. It has existed for years. In fact, the Colombo meeting was not even the first such engagement after Operation Sindoor. It was at least the fifth. Before Colombo, there had already been meetings in London, Muscat, Thailand and Doha. The first two would be described by Pakistani participants as Track 1.5, while the latter two were Track II. Whatever label one chooses to use, the engagement itself was not new.

What made the Colombo meeting noteworthy was not that it took place, but that details of it entered the public domain. That happened because some of the participants themselves left enough clues through their travel and social media activity for the pieces to be put together. Once those breadcrumbs were matched with the conference timeline, the picture became fairly clear.

After Operation Sindoor and the government’s repeated assertion that ‘talks and terror cannot go together’, many would reasonably have expected even these informal channels to have been suspended. Reports that such engagement continued even after Operation Sindoor therefore raised legitimate public interest.

What is perhaps more worrying, however, is the growing tendency in our public discourse to dismiss inconvenient but accurate reporting as ‘propaganda’ or ‘PSYOP’, rather than engage with the facts. Instead of addressing what is being reported, the instinct is to shoot the messenger. That does little to improve the quality of public debate.

There is another important distinction. Track II is not government-to-government negotiation. But it is equally unrealistic to pretend that sustained India-Pakistan Track II engagements involving prominent former officials, public intellectuals, and strategic figures occur without the knowledge of the respective governments. These dialogues are unofficial, not clandestine.

Whether one chooses to call it Track II or Track 1.5, as some in Pakistan do, is beside the point. These channels have existed for years, and their existence is very easily independently verifiable.

Public debate is healthier when we distinguish between official diplomacy, Track II dialogue and back-channel engagement, instead of conflating them. Calling factual reporting about Track II ‘propaganda’ does not change the long-established reality that these channels have existed alongside periods of frozen official relations.
summary: Argues Track II India-Pakistan dialogues continued after Op Sindoor despite denials.

author: @raghavwadhwa
text:
DAC has cleared ₹52,000 crore worth of defence acquisition proposals.

But this is not just another "defence sector positive" headline.

This approval clearly shows where India's next defence capex cycle is moving:

Drones. Anti-drone systems. Air defence. Missiles. Electronic warfare. Surveillance. Unmanned warfare. Naval autonomous systems.

India just closed a financial year where record order books sat next to falling revenue. In FY26 the DAC granted acceptances worth about ₹6.73 lakh crore, but contracts actually signed came to ₹2.28 lakh crore. Approval is not money. The real edge this cycle is not spotting the beneficiary, it is spotting who converts an order book into billed revenue.

Here is the map, with the number that matters next to each name.
🔹 Missiles: MRSAM, V-SHORADS, MPATGM
🔸 Bharat Dynamics is the production agency for all three, the most direct listed missile play. But the conversion is stuck: FY26 revenue fell 27% to ₹2,442 crore, inventory rose 75% to ₹4,626 crore, and Motilal Oswal pegged ₹2,000 crore of the revenue miss to delivery delays on Akash and Astra Mk-1 alone.
🔸 MRSAM carries significant imported Israeli content, so part of the headline value leaves the country. Not a clean indigenous play.
🔸 Premier Explosives is the quiet pick and shovel, the only Indian name qualified for solid propellants and countermeasures, feeding the Akash, Astra and long range SAM class plus BrahMos boosters. Order book around ₹1,569 crore, over four times FY26 revenue.

🔹 Defence electronics, radar, EW and optics: Akash Tarang, fire control, active protection
🔸 Bharat Electronics productionises the DRDO D4 counter-drone system and builds the radar and EW layer. Order book ₹74,453 crore as of September 2025, and it is on the right side of the conversion gap, still growing revenue while platform makers stall.
🔸 Paras Defence is the one most lists underweight. It is the only Indian firm making infrared optics at scale, the seeker and electro-optic layer inside air defence, loitering munitions and tank sights. Order book ₹986 crore, up from ₹215 crore in FY21, with a ₹52.82 crore electro-optics order from BEL and an in-principle demerger of its space and meteorology arm that could unlock a separate listed pure-play.
🔸 Astra Microwave sits in the RF and microwave sensing layer of these missiles and radars. Order visibility above ₹1,600 crore, one of the few that kept converting in FY26, though one brokerage rates it Reduce on valuation.
🔸 Centum Electronics runs defence electronics, avionics and EW modules. Order book ₹1,645 crore, up 23%, but read the FY26 bottom line carefully, it was distorted by a ₹203 crore one-time exceptional from overseas subsidiaries, so operating health is better than the headline profit.
🔸 Data Patterns builds radar, EW and C4ISR electronics, a direct read on the EW content. Worth pulling its latest concall order book before sizing it.
🔸 DCX Systems does system integration and harnesses for radar, missiles and EW. It carries the biggest book of the small caps at ₹2,984 crore, but it is also the sharpest warning sign: FY26 revenue fell to ₹743 crore with a small loss. Large book, weak delivery.

🔹 Loitering munitions and anti-drone: jet-based kamikaze drones
🔸 Solar Industries is the standout. It makes the Nagastra loitering munition and Bhargavastra anti-drone system, has committed roughly ₹10,000 crore of defence capex over the decade, and is the clearest case of conversion actually happening: FY26 defence revenue up 94% to ₹2,634 crore.
🔸 Zen Technologies is the pure counter-drone and layered kill play, order book ₹1,336 crore into FY27. But it sits on the wrong side of conversion for now, FY26 revenue down 29% to ₹688 crore with Q4 down roughly 45% on order timing.
🔸 ideaForge is the listed ISR drone leader, with its highest ever order inflows this cycle taking the book to around ₹360 crore. Real, but smaller than the drone noise suggests.

🔹 The naval mine most lists get wrong: MIGM
🔸 Apollo Micro Systems is the DRDO approved production agency for the MIGM Vighana under the DcPP framework, technology transferred in August 2025. It also holds a DPIIT lifetime arms licence from April 2026 covering missiles, ATGMs, torpedoes and loitering munitions, quietly placing it behind several systems in this same clearance.

🔹 Naval propulsion and high altitude ISR: LBTF, FW-HAPS
🔸 The electric propulsion testing facility and the pseudo satellite are real capability, but there is no clean listed pure-play. That work still sits mostly inside DRDO and NAL, and the large, diversified names people attach here have negligible exposure. Honest gap, not a thesis.
The conversion scorecard, which is the actual insight:

FY26 split the listed field into two camps.
🔸 Converting: BEL, Solar Industries, Astra Microwave, Mazagon Dock. Component and consumables suppliers who bill off advance pools and do not wait on platform acceptance.

🔸 Stuck: Bharat Dynamics, HAL (order book ₹2.54 lakh crore but revenue up just 7%), Bharat Forge Defence, Zen Technologies, and on current numbers DCX. Complex platform and integration names whose books grow while revenue falls and inventory climbs.

That split, not the AoN headline, is what this ₹52,000 crore actually rewards over the next few years. Names like Nibe and BEML sit on the generic lists but do not clear the qualified vendor test on these specific systems, so treat them as theme exposure, not production agencies.

What to watch in FY27, in order: AoN to contract, contract to delivery, delivery to billing, billing to cash. The company that shortens those four ratios earns the re-rating, however long its order book looks today.

text:
🇬🇷🇮🇳 Greece and India Draw Closer: A Partnership That Has Turkey Watching Closely

India and Greece are strengthening their ties, which has caused concern in Turkey. Though the two countries are separated by vast distances, recent moves in defense, trade, and diplomacy are bringing them together and reshaping dynamics in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The relationship gained noticeable momentum in early 2026. Greek Defense Minister Nikos Dendias met with India's Rajnath Singh in New Delhi, where they signed documents outlining future defense industry cooperation and a military cooperation plan for the year. No major arms deals were announced on the spot, but the talks themselves carried weight—particularly regarding the possibility of India exporting advanced systems like the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile to Greece or Cyprus.

This is built on earlier steps. In 2023, Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Greece—the first such trip by an Indian leader in decades—and the two nations upgraded their relationship to a strategic partnership. What started as diplomatic warming has since taken on more practical elements, including joint military exercises, staff talks, and discussions about port infrastructure.

The Missile That Changes the Conversation

Much of the attention has focused on the BrahMos, a fast, jointly developed Indo-Russian supersonic cruise missile. Capable of traveling at nearly three times the speed of sound and flying low over the sea in its final approach, it leaves limited reaction time for defenders—around 90 seconds in ideal conditions.

In the crowded waters of the Aegean, where the Greek islands are close and shipping routes overlap, that kind of capability could complicate naval planning. Turkish analysts have publicly noted that even the prospect of Greece fielding such a system would force a rethink of regional military balances. Deployment details remain hypothetical, but the geography favors positions that are protected yet able to cover key approaches, turning certain islands into potential long-range strike platforms.

For now, no missiles have been transferred. Still, the conversation alone is enough to influence how Turkish planners think about sea control and deterrence.

Trade Routes and Economic Strategy

Beyond weapons, economics is playing a big role. India is pushing the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (I-MEC), a project designed to link Indian ports through the Gulf and Israel to Greek harbors like Piraeus, then into the rest of Europe. The route is intended to speed up cargo movement and cut costs compared to traditional paths through the Suez Canal—and notably, it avoids Turkish territory.

Greek leaders have expressed support for the initiative, and both countries see potential in expanding port facilities, particularly in northern Greece, to handle more Indian trade. For Turkey, which has long benefited from its position astride key land and sea routes between Asia and Europe, alternative corridors represent a slow erosion of that geographic advantage.

Shared Concerns and Wider Connections

Tensions between India and Turkey have grown in recent years, especially after Turkey supported Pakistan during Operation Sindoor following the deadly Pahalham terror attack in Kashmir. Turkey's clear stance in favor of Pakistan accelerated India's efforts to build ties elsewhere.

Turkey, which occupies the northern portion of Cyprus and claims Greece's maritime space, is not in the crosshairs of India. India has also deepened defense cooperation with Armenia, supplying artillery, missiles, and other equipment worth nearly $2 billion in recent years. These relationships do not form a formal military bloc, but they create overlapping interests among countries that all have reasons to be wary of Turkish influence.

Joint India-Greece air and naval exercises have taken place, and military-to-military contacts are becoming more routine. The result is a web of practical cooperation rather than a grand alliance with mutual defense guarantees.

A Different Kind of Partnership

What’s happening does not fit neatly into old Cold War frameworks. India, a non-NATO country with strong defense ties to the United States, is engaging more deeply with Greece—a NATO member—on issues that indirectly concern another NATO member, Turkey. So far, there has been little public pushback from Washington.

Analysts describe this as an “alignment of interests” rather than a formal treaty. It’s flexible, focused on specific goals like secure trade routes and military modernization, and driven by mutual opportunities rather than ideology.

Turkey has responded with diplomatic outreach to India and statements emphasizing dialogue. This will obviously not lead to eased tensions as India now knows Turkey's duplicitous games by sending drones and drone operators to kill Indians during Operation Sindoor.

For now, the Eastern Mediterranean is seeing a gradual shift: new trade paths, closer defense conversations, and countries finding common ground in unexpected places.

The partnership between India and Greece is still developing, but it already highlights how they are capable of countering Turkey's plans for grandeur - a neo-Turkic Empire spanning from the Eastern Mediterranean to the Indian subcontinent. Turkey wanted to bring problems to India, now India is knocking on Turkey's doorstep.

author: @SpencerGuard
text:
One of the most remarkable moments in American history came on July 4, 1826, the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. 🇺🇸

On that day, two of the nation's Founding Fathers and former Presidents, Thomas Jefferson and John Adams, passed away within hours of one another. Jefferson, the principal author of the Declaration, died at Monticello at age 83. Adams, who fiercely defended and helped secure America's independence, died later that day in Massachusetts at age 90.

Their passing on the nation's Jubilee seemed to symbolize the completion of a generation's work. They had devoted their lives to the cause of liberty, lived to witness the United States reach its first half-century, and left behind a republic whose ideals continue to inspire the world.

As we celebrate Independence Day, it's worth remembering not only how America was founded, but the extraordinary men whose vision, sacrifice, and perseverance made it possible.

Happy Birthday, America. 🇺🇸
summary: Recounts Jefferson and Adams deaths on 1826 Independence Day anniversary.

🚨 IAF displays S-400 missile debris linked to Operation Sindoor

The Indian Air Force has displayed what is believed to be debris from a 40N6 interceptor missile used by the S-400 air defence system during Operation Sindoor.

The displayed part reportedly carries serial markings that identify it as a component of the S-400’s long-range missile.

According to the IAF, this missile was used in a 314 km surface-to-air engagement, which it says is the longest surface-to-air kill ever recorded.

The Air Force has not officially revealed the identity of the target. However, several defence reports have claimed it was a high-value Pakistan Air Force aircraft. Those claims have not been independently verified.

If the IAF’s account is accurate, it would be one of the most significant long-range air defence engagements in modern military history.

author: @thegeo_sync
text:
🔴Fresh evidence is adding a new twist to the debate over Pakistan’s claim that it destroyed India’s S-400 air defence system during Operation Sindoor.

A newly surfaced image, reportedly taken on 10 May, shows an Indian Air Force S-400 launcher firing a missile during the operation. The timing is important because Pakistan had claimed the S-400 battery at Adampur was destroyed on that very day.

India rejected that claim from the beginning, calling it false. A few days later, Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Adampur Air Base, and images from the visit showed an S-400 launcher in the background. At the time, many saw it as India’s way of countering Pakistan’s narrative.

Now, this newly released image adds another piece of evidence. If it is authentic, it suggests the S-400 was not only intact but also actively engaged in combat operations on 10 May.

The discussion doesn’t end there. During Operation Sindoor, the Indian Air Force later stated that it achieved its longest-ever publicly acknowledged surface-to-air engagement, at a range of around 314 km. While officials have not revealed every operational detail, many defence observers believe the S-400 played a key role in that engagement.

Taken together, the available evidence paints a different picture from Pakistan’s original claim. Instead of being destroyed, the S-400 appears to have remained operational throughout the conflict and may have been one of India’s most important assets during Operation Sindoor.

As always, independent verification of every battlefield claim is difficult. But with each new image and official disclosure, Pakistan’s claim of destroying India’s S-400 appears increasingly difficult to support.

author: @Defence_Squad_
text:
Ukraine’s reported strikes on Russian S-400 launchers carry a lesson, but India is not starting from zero.

India already fields a layered air-defence architecture, with systems such as the S-400, Akash and MRSAM, backed by increasingly networked command-and-control.

During Operation Sindoor, the Army’s Akashteer worked with the IAF’s IACCS and Navy’s Trigun to create a unified real-time operational picture.

India is now pushing this approach further through Mission Sudarshan Chakra, envisioned as a multi-level missile defence system protecting critical military and civilian infrastructure.

The lesson from Ukraine is not that the S-400 is obsolete. It is that survivability depends on integration, mobility, electronic warfare, counter-drone protection and layered defence.

India has built the foundations. The priority now is to expand, harden and integrate them faster.
